rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Which of the following does not show variable oxidation states ?
rows.solution:
SCANDIUM does not show variable oxidation states.

Scandium is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^1 4s^2\). Losing all three of those electrons gives \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\), which has the argon configuration — an EMPTY \(3d\) subshell, with nothing further to give and no partly filled set to fall back to. Scandium has no other stable state, and its \(+3\) compounds are white and diamagnetic, unlike the coloured paramagnetic compounds of the rest of the series.

The other three are all variable: iron shows \(+2\) and \(+3\), copper \(+1\) and \(+2\), and manganese the whole run from \(+2\) to \(+7\).

Variable oxidation states arise because the \((n-1)d\) and \(ns\) subshells lie at comparable energies, so electrons from both are available — and scandium simply has too few d electrons for that to give it any choice.

rows.stem: The type of isomerism shown by the complex \([\mathrm{CoCl_2(en)_2}]^{+}\) is :
rows.solution:
The complex shows GEOMETRICAL ISOMERISM.

\(\mathrm{[CoCl_2(en)_2]^{+}}\) is octahedral with two chlorido ligands and two bidentate diamines — the type \(\mathrm{MA_2(BB)_2}\). The two chlorides may sit ADJACENT, giving the CIS isomer, or OPPOSITE each other, giving the TRANS isomer.

The other three need something this complex does not have. LINKAGE isomerism needs an ambidentate ligand, and neither chloride nor the diamine is one. COORDINATION isomerism needs both the cation and the anion to be complex ions. IONISATION isomerism needs a counter ion that could change places with a ligand.

The cis form is also OPTICALLY active, having no plane of symmetry, so this complex shows optical isomerism as well — but only geometrical isomerism is offered.

rows.stem:
Which of the following is diamagnetic in nature ?
[Atomic number : Co = 27]

options.label: A
options.text: \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\), octahedral complex with strong field ligand

options.label: B
options.text: \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\), octahedral complex with weak field ligand

rows.solution:
The diamagnetic one is the OCTAHEDRAL complex with a STRONG FIELD LIGAND.

Cobalt is atomic number 27, so \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) is \(3d^6\) — six electrons in five orbitals, which leaves four unpaired if they spread out.

A STRONG field ligand in an OCTAHEDRAL field splits the d orbitals widely, so \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}}\) exceeds the pairing energy and all six electrons crowd into the three lower \(t_{2g}\) orbitals: \(t_{2g}^6\,e_g^0\). Every electron is paired, so the complex is DIAMAGNETIC.

A WEAK field ligand leaves the splitting too small to force pairing, giving \(t_{2g}^4\,e_g^2\) with four unpaired electrons — paramagnetic. Tetrahedral complexes split even less and are always high spin, so that option is paramagnetic too. And a \(d^6\) square planar complex leaves one unpaired electron in the highest orbital.

rows.stem:
Consider the following reaction :
\(\mathrm{Cl-C_6H_4-CH_2-Cl} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KCN}} ?\)
The major product of the reaction is :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — REQUIRED - the reactant in the stem AND ALL FOUR options are printed as DRAWN benzene-ring structures, not as formulae. On the page: the reactant is a ring bearing -CH2-Cl and, para to it, -Cl; (A) a ring bearing -CH2-CN and, para, -CN; (B) a ring bearing -CH2-Cl and, para, -CN; (C) a ring bearing -CH2-CN and, para, -Cl; (D) a TRISUBSTITUTED ring bearing -CH2-CN, -Cl para to it, and a third -CN on the ring carbon adjacent to the Cl. The condensed formulae above record substituent identity faithfully but cannot express the ring positions, and (D)'s especially - it is written 'Cl-C6H3(CN)-CH2-CN' only to keep the four options distinguishable. Attach the real crop. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
The major product is \(\mathrm{Cl{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_2{-}CN}\).

The molecule carries TWO chlorines in quite different positions, and cyanide can displace only one of them.

The side-chain chlorine is BENZYLIC — on an \(sp^3\) carbon attached to the ring — and benzylic halides are unusually reactive, their carbocation being stabilised by resonance with the ring. Cyanide displaces it readily.

The ring chlorine is ARYL. Its lone pair is delocalised into the ring, so the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond has partial double bond character, and the carbon holding it is \(sp^2\) and more electronegative. Displacing it needs about 623 K and 300 atmospheres, conditions far beyond what this reaction uses.

So the cyanide attacks the side chain and the ring chlorine is untouched. The two options that substitute on the ring both ignore that difference.

rows.stem: Which one of the following compounds has the lowest \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) value ?
rows.solution:
The LOWEST \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) — meaning the STRONGEST acid — belongs to 2,4,6-TRINITROPHENOL, picric acid.

Acidity here is decided by what the substituents do to the PHENOXIDE ion left behind. Electron-WITHDRAWING groups help disperse its negative charge, stabilise it, and make the proton leave more readily.

Picric acid carries THREE nitro groups, and their positions matter as much as their number: two ortho and one para, all three able to take the negative charge onto their own oxygens by resonance. The combined effect is enormous — \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) about 0.4, which makes picric acid a genuinely strong acid, comparable to a mineral acid.

p-Nitrophenol has one such group and comes in at about 7.1. m-Nitrophenol's group is META, where resonance cannot reach, so only the inductive pull operates and it manages about 8.4. And p-cresol's methyl group RELEASES electron density, making it WEAKER than phenol itself at about 10.2.

rows.stem: \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-O-CH_3}\) when treated with HI gives :
rows.solution:
The products are ISOPROPYL ALCOHOL AND METHYL IODIDE, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH{-}OH} + \mathrm{CH_3{-}I}\).

Neither group here is tertiary — one is secondary and one primary — so the cleavage goes by the BIMOLECULAR route. The acid protonates the ether, and the iodide then attacks the carbon it can reach most easily, which is the LESS HINDERED one.

Of a methyl group and an isopropyl group, the methyl is far the less hindered. So the iodine goes to the METHYL carbon and the isopropyl group keeps the oxygen:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CH{-}O{-}CH_3} + \mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CH{-}OH} + \mathrm{CH_3I}\)

The contrast with a TERTIARY ether is worth holding. There the protonated ether falls apart to a stable tertiary carbocation, the route is unimolecular, and the iodide goes to the MORE substituted carbon instead — the opposite pairing, from the same reagent.

rows.stem: Which of the following compounds on treatment with benzene sulphonyl choride forms an alkali-soluble precipitate ?
rows.solution:
The compound is ETHYLAMINE, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}\).

Benzenesulphonyl chloride is Hinsberg's reagent, and the test turns on how many hydrogens remain on the nitrogen after it reacts.

A PRIMARY amine gives a sulphonamide that still has ONE hydrogen on its nitrogen. That hydrogen is made acidic by the two electron-withdrawing oxygens of the sulphonyl group beside it, so the precipitate DISSOLVES in alkali as its sodium salt — exactly what the question describes.

A SECONDARY amine gives a sulphonamide with NO hydrogen left on nitrogen, so its precipitate is insoluble in alkali; dimethylamine falls here. A TERTIARY amine has no nitrogen-hydrogen bond at all and does not react, so trimethylamine gives no precipitate to test.

Acetamide is not an amine but an AMIDE. Its nitrogen's lone pair is already delocalised onto the carbonyl oxygen, leaving it far too poor a nucleophile to attack the sulphonyl chloride.

rows.stem: The order of increasing basicities of \(\mathrm{CH_3NH_2}\) (I), \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2NH}\) (II), \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N}\) (III) and \(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\) (IV) in aqueous media is :
rows.solution:
Increasing basicity in AQUEOUS media runs
\(\mathrm{IV} < \mathrm{III} < \mathrm{I} < \mathrm{II}\)
that is, aniline, then trimethylamine, then methylamine, then dimethylamine.

ANILINE is much the weakest and is easily placed first: its nitrogen's lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is far less available to accept a proton.

Among the three methylamines the order is not a simple progression, because three effects compete. Methyl groups RELEASE electron density onto the nitrogen, which favours the tertiary amine. But the cation formed on protonation must also be STABILISED BY HYDROGEN BONDING to the surrounding water, and that needs hydrogens on the nitrogen — the tertiary amine's cation has only one, and its three methyl groups crowd the water away besides.

The SECONDARY amine is the compromise that wins: two methyl groups pushing electrons in, and still one hydrogen available for solvation. The tertiary amine comes LAST of the three on both solvation counts.

The qualification "in aqueous media" is load-bearing. In the GAS PHASE there is no solvent to stabilise anything, only the inductive effect operates, and the order becomes simply primary, secondary, tertiary.

rows.stem: The vitamin which plays an important role in coagulating blood is :
rows.solution:
VITAMIN K plays the important role in coagulating blood.

It is needed to make several of the clotting factors, so a deficiency shows as an increased CLOTTING TIME — cuts bleed for longer, and bruising is easy. Vitamin K is FAT SOLUBLE, so the body can store a reserve of it, and newborns, who have little, are routinely given a dose.

Of the others: vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia, vitamin D deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults, and vitamin E deficiency causes increased fragility of red blood cells.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: When a catalyst increases the rate of a chemical reaction, then the rate constant (k) :

options.label: D
options.text: may increase or decrease depending on the order of the reaction

rows.solution:
The RATE CONSTANT INCREASES.

A catalyst works by offering the reaction an ALTERNATIVE PATH with a LOWER ACTIVATION ENERGY. By the Arrhenius equation
\(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\)
a smaller \(E_a\) makes the exponential term larger, so \(k\) itself is larger.

That is in fact the only way the rate CAN rise here. Adding a catalyst changes none of the concentrations, so in \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^m[\mathrm{B}]^n\) the concentration factors are exactly what they were. If the rate has gone up, the constant must have gone up with it.

What a catalyst does NOT change is the position of equilibrium. It leaves \(\Delta H\), \(\Delta S\) and \(\Delta G\) untouched, and it lowers the barrier in both directions equally, so the equilibrium constant is unchanged — the reaction simply reaches the same equilibrium sooner.

[The marking scheme keys this question as "remains constant". That reading cannot be reconciled with the Arrhenius equation: lowering the activation energy is precisely what raises \(k\), and with the concentrations unchanged there is nothing else for a faster rate to come from. The bank's stored key follows the scheme.]

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: A 1% solution of solute 'X' is isotonic with a 6% solution of sucrose (molar mass = 342 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)). The molar mass of solute 'X' is :
rows.solution:
ISOTONIC means the two solutions have the SAME osmotic pressure. Since \(\Pi = CRT\) and both are at the same temperature, equal osmotic pressure means equal MOLAR CONCENTRATION.

Both percentages are mass per unit volume and refer to the same volume, so the concentrations may be compared as mass divided by molar mass:
\(\dfrac{w_{\mathrm{X}}}{M_{\mathrm{X}}} = \dfrac{w_{\text{sucrose}}}{M_{\text{sucrose}}}\)
\(\dfrac{1}{M_{\mathrm{X}}} = \dfrac{6}{342}\)

\(M_{\mathrm{X}} = \dfrac{342}{6} = 57\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

The result is worth a sanity check: solute \(\mathrm{X}\) is present at only a SIXTH of the sucrose's mass yet supplies the same number of moles, so its molar mass must be a sixth of sucrose's — and it is. Note also that neither answer depends on knowing the temperature, since it cancels from both sides.

rows.stem: During the electrolysis of aqueous NaCl, the cathodic reaction is :
rows.solution:
The cathodic reaction is the REDUCTION OF WATER.

The cathode is where reduction happens, and the two candidates are the sodium ion and water:
\(\mathrm{Na^+} + e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na}\), \(E^{\circ} = -2{\cdot}71\) V
\(2\mathrm{H_2O} + 2e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{H_2} + 2\mathrm{OH^-}\), \(E^{\circ} = -0{\cdot}83\) V

The species with the HIGHER reduction potential is reduced preferentially, and \(-0{\cdot}83\) is far higher than \(-2{\cdot}71\). Water is reduced, hydrogen gas is evolved, and the sodium ion stays in solution.

The two OXIDATION options are excluded by the word CATHODIC alone — oxidation happens at the anode. And it is worth knowing which oxidation wins there: chlorine, not water, because liberating oxygen carries a substantial overpotential that wipes out its small thermodynamic advantage.

The hydroxide left behind is why the solution turns alkaline as the electrolysis proceeds.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Addition of ethylene glycol to water lowers its freezing point.
Reason (R) : Ethylene glycol is insoluble in water due to lack of its ability to form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Ethylene glycol does lower the freezing point of water — that is exactly why it is used as antifreeze in car radiators, and the effect is a colligative one, depending on the number of solute particles.

The Reason has the solubility precisely backwards. Ethylene glycol carries TWO hydroxyl groups and hydrogen bonds to water extremely well; it is MISCIBLE with water in all proportions.

And the correction restores the argument. A solute must DISSOLVE before it can depress anything: an insoluble substance sitting at the bottom of the flask would leave the freezing point exactly where it was. So the Reason as written would predict no depression at all — the opposite of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Order of reaction and molecularity are always same for complex reactions.
Reason (R) : Order is determined experimentally and molecularity is applicable only for elementary reactions.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is FALSE while the Reason is TRUE.

Order and molecularity are NOT always the same for complex reactions — for a complex reaction molecularity is not even defined, so they cannot be compared at all.

The Reason states the two facts that make the Assertion false. ORDER is determined EXPERIMENTALLY, from how the measured rate responds when concentrations are changed. MOLECULARITY is a theoretical count of the species that must collide in an ELEMENTARY step, and a complex reaction is a SEQUENCE of steps, each possibly with its own molecularity — so the sequence as a whole has none to quote.

The two coincide only for an ELEMENTARY reaction, where the single step IS the reaction. That is the exception the Assertion has turned into a rule.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The boiling point of ethanol is higher than that of dimethyl ether.
Reason (R) : Ethanol molecules are associated through hydrogen bonding whereas in dimethyl ether, it is not possible.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Ethanol and dimethyl ether are isomers — both \(\mathrm{C_2H_6O}\), the same mass, the same number of electrons — so the enormous gap in their boiling points, 351 K against 248 K, cannot come from size.

It comes from HYDROGEN BONDING, exactly as the Reason says. Ethanol's hydrogen sits on OXYGEN, so its molecules associate strongly with one another and a great deal of energy is needed to separate them. Dimethyl ether has no hydrogen on an electronegative atom at all — both are on carbon — so its molecules can only manage weak dipole-dipole attraction.

The ether's oxygen can still ACCEPT a hydrogen bond, which is why dimethyl ether dissolves in water; what it cannot do is DONATE one, and hydrogen bonding between like molecules needs both.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Aniline does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reaction.
Reason (R) : Friedel-Crafts reaction is an electrophilic substitution reaction.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Aniline does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reaction, and Friedel-Crafts IS an electrophilic substitution — both statements hold.

But the second does not account for the first. Being an electrophilic substitution is a property of the REACTION, true of benzene and toluene as much as of aniline, and those both undergo it perfectly well. It cannot explain why this particular substrate fails.

The real reason concerns the CATALYST. Aluminium chloride is a Lewis acid, and the nitrogen's lone pair is exactly what it seeks — so it bonds to the nitrogen and is tied up. Worse, the nitrogen is now positively charged, and a positively charged group is strongly deactivating and meta directing, so the ring can barely react at all.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: Define molal depression constant. How is it related to enthalpy of fusion ?
rows.solution:
MOLAL DEPRESSION CONSTANT, \(K_f\), is the depression in freezing point produced when ONE MOLE of a non-volatile solute is dissolved in ONE KILOGRAM of the solvent — that is, the depression shown by a one molal solution. It is also called the cryoscopic constant, and for water it is \(1{\cdot}86\) K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\).

It is a property of the SOLVENT alone, not of the solute, which is what makes \(\Delta T_f = K_f\,m\) a colligative relation.

RELATION TO THE ENTHALPY OF FUSION:
\(K_f = \dfrac{R \times M_{\text{solvent}} \times T_f^{\,2}}{1000 \times \Delta_{\text{fus}}H}\)

where \(T_f\) is the freezing point of the pure solvent in kelvin, \(M_{\text{solvent}}\) its molar mass and \(\Delta_{\text{fus}}H\) its enthalpy of fusion.

Note the INVERSE dependence: a solvent that is hard to melt, with a large enthalpy of fusion, has a SMALL \(K_f\) and shows only a slight depression. Camphor is the opposite extreme, with \(K_f\) near 40, which is why it is used when a large, easily measured depression is wanted.

rows.stem: What type of deviation is shown by ethanol and acetone mixture ? Give reason. What type of azeotropic mixture is formed by that deviation ?
rows.solution:
A mixture of ethanol and acetone shows a POSITIVE DEVIATION from Raoult's law.

WHY. Pure ethanol is extensively hydrogen bonded to itself. Adding acetone puts acetone molecules between the ethanol molecules and breaks some of those hydrogen bonds, and acetone cannot replace them in kind — it has no hydrogen on oxygen to donate, only a lone pair to accept with.

So the interactions between UNLIKE molecules are WEAKER than those between the like molecules of pure ethanol. Held less tightly, the molecules escape more readily than Raoult's law predicts, and the observed vapour pressure is HIGHER than the ideal value. Mixing is endothermic and the volume expands slightly — the same fact seen from two other directions.

TYPE OF AZEOTROPE: a MINIMUM BOILING azeotrope. Higher vapour pressure means a lower boiling point, so the mixture at the azeotropic composition boils BELOW either pure component.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
(a) In a reaction, if the concentration of reactant 'X' is tripled, the rate of reaction becomes twenty-seven times. What is the order of the reaction ?
(b) State a condition under which a bimolecular reaction is kinetically a first-order reaction. Give an example of such a reaction.
rows.solution:
(a) The rate responds to concentration as \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{X}]^p\), so multiplying the concentration by 3 multiplies the rate by \(3^p\):
\(27 = 3^{p}\)
and since \(27 = 3^3\), the order is THREE.

Reading the exponent off the numbers is the whole method, and it works whatever the stoichiometry says — order is a property of the MECHANISM, and has to be measured.

(b) CONDITION: a bimolecular reaction becomes kinetically FIRST ORDER when ONE OF THE REACTANTS IS PRESENT IN LARGE EXCESS.

Its concentration then barely changes as the reaction proceeds, so it can be treated as a constant and absorbed into the rate constant. What remains depends on one concentration alone.

EXAMPLE: the acid hydrolysis of an ester, where water is the solvent as well as a reactant:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COOC_2H_5} + \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{CH_3COOH} + \mathrm{C_2H_5OH}\)
\(\text{Rate} = k[\text{ester}][\mathrm{H_2O}] = k'[\text{ester}]\) with \(k' = k[\mathrm{H_2O}]\)

Such a reaction is called PSEUDO first order — bimolecular by its stoichiometry, first order by measurement. The inversion of sucrose is another instance.

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem:
Complete the following ionic equations :
(a) \(\mathrm{2MnO_4^{-} + 5SO_3^{2-} + 6H^{+} \longrightarrow}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 14H^{+} + 6Fe^{2+} \longrightarrow}\)
rows.solution:
(a) Permanganate oxidises sulphite to sulphate in acid, manganese falling from \(+7\) to \(+2\):
\(2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 5\mathrm{SO_3^{2-}} + 6\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 5\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Ten electrons change hands: two permanganates take five each, and five sulphites give up two each as sulphur rises from \(+4\) to \(+6\). The charge balances at \(-6\) on both sides, which is the quickest check.

(b) Dichromate oxidises iron(II) to iron(III) in acid, chromium falling from \(+6\) to \(+3\):
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 14\mathrm{H^+} + 6\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 6\mathrm{Fe^{3+}} + 7\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Six electrons change hands: two chromiums take three each, and six iron(II) ions give up one each. This reaction is the basis of the volumetric estimation of iron, dichromate being a primary standard.

rows.stem:
(a) Which halogen compound in the following pair will react faster in \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) reactions and why ?
\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-I}\)   OR   \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-Br}\)
(b) Why is chloroform stored in closed dark coloured bottles ?
rows.solution:
(a) IODOETHANE, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2I}\), reacts faster.

With the same carbon skeleton in both, the only variable is how good a leaving group the halogen makes. In an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction the carbon-halogen bond breaks as the nucleophile attacks, so the WEAKER that bond, the faster the reaction.

The \(\mathrm{C-I}\) bond is weaker than the \(\mathrm{C-Br}\) bond, because iodine is the larger atom and its orbital overlaps carbon's less well. The iodide ion is also the more stable of the two anions, being larger and better able to spread its charge — a better leaving group in both senses.

(b) Because chloroform is slowly OXIDISED BY AIR IN THE PRESENCE OF LIGHT to PHOSGENE, \(\mathrm{COCl_2}\), which is extremely poisonous:
\(2\mathrm{CHCl_3} + \mathrm{O_2} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} 2\mathrm{COCl_2} + 2\mathrm{HCl}\)

A dark bottle keeps the light out and a closed one keeps the air out, so each stopper blocks one of the two requirements. As a further precaution chloroform is stored nearly full, leaving little air inside, and about 1% ethanol is added — it destroys any phosgene formed by converting it to the harmless diethyl carbonate.

rows.stem:
Give reaction of glucose with the following :
(a) HCN
(b) Conc. \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\)
rows.solution:
(a) WITH HYDROGEN CYANIDE, glucose forms a CYANOHYDRIN — the cyanide adds to the carbonyl carbon and the hydrogen to the oxygen:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} + \mathrm{HCN} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH(OH)(CN)(CHOH)_4CH_2OH}\)

The product has SEVEN carbons where the sugar had six. That this nucleophilic addition works at all is one of the proofs that glucose contains a carbonyl group.

(b) WITH CONCENTRATED NITRIC ACID, a strong oxidising agent, BOTH ends of the molecule are oxidised — the aldehyde at \(\mathrm{C_1}\) and the primary alcohol at \(\mathrm{C_6}\) — giving the dicarboxylic SACCHARIC ACID:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. }\mathrm{HNO_3}} \mathrm{COOH(CHOH)_4COOH}\)

The contrast with bromine water is the point. That milder reagent touches only the aldehyde and gives gluconic acid, a MONOcarboxylic acid — which is how the primary hydroxyl at the far end is established separately.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem:
A solution is prepared by dissolving 5 g of a non-volatile solute in 200 g of water. It has a vapour pressure of \(31{\cdot}84\) mm Hg at 300 K. Calculate the molar mass of the solute.
(Vapour pressure of pure water at 300 K = 32 mm Hg)
rows.solution:
Raoult's law for a non-volatile solute in a dilute solution relates the relative lowering of vapour pressure to the mole ratio of solute to solvent:
\(\dfrac{p_1^{\,\circ} - p_1}{p_1^{\,\circ}} = \dfrac{w_2 \times M_1}{M_2 \times w_1}\)

Substituting the data — solvent water with \(M_1 = 18\), \(w_1 = 200\) g, solute \(w_2 = 5\) g:
\(\dfrac{32 - 31{\cdot}84}{32} = \dfrac{5 \times 18}{M_2 \times 200}\)
\(\dfrac{0{\cdot}16}{32} = \dfrac{90}{200\,M_2}\)
\(0{\cdot}005 = \dfrac{0{\cdot}45}{M_2}\)

\(M_2 = \dfrac{0{\cdot}45}{0{\cdot}005} = 90\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

Note how small the lowering is — 0.16 mm Hg out of 32, a half of one per cent. That is what makes this measurement demanding in practice, and it is why osmotic pressure is preferred for macromolecules, where the effect would be smaller still.

rows.stem:
The conductivity of \(0{\cdot}2\) M solution of KCl is \(2{\cdot}48 \times 10^{-2}\) S \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\). Calculate its molar conductivity and degree of dissociation \((\alpha)\).
Given :
\(\lambda^{o}_{\mathrm{K^{+}}} = 73{\cdot}5\) S \(\mathrm{cm^{2}\,mol^{-1}}\)
\(\lambda^{o}_{\mathrm{Cl^{-}}} = 76{\cdot}5\) S \(\mathrm{cm^{2}\,mol^{-1}}\)
rows.solution:
MOLAR CONDUCTIVITY. Conductivity is a property of a fixed volume; molar conductivity refers it to one mole of electrolyte, so the concentration divides out:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{C} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}48 \times 10^{-2} \times 1000}{0{\cdot}2}\)

\(\Lambda_m = 124\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

DEGREE OF DISSOCIATION. At infinite dilution the electrolyte is fully dissociated, and by Kohlrausch's law the limiting value is the sum of the two ionic contributions:
\(\Lambda_m^{\circ} = \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{K^+}} + \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cl^-}} = 73{\cdot}5 + 76{\cdot}5 = 150\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

The degree of dissociation is the ratio of the two:
\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^{\circ}} = \dfrac{124}{150}\)

\(\alpha = 0{\cdot}827\), about 83%

The figure is worth reading: potassium chloride is a STRONG electrolyte and is fully ionised in solution, so the shortfall from 1 here is not incomplete dissociation at all but the drag that ions exert on one another at this concentration. For a WEAK electrolyte the same ratio really does measure how much has dissociated.

rows.stem:
A first-order reaction is 25% complete in 40 minutes. Calculate the value of rate constant. In what time will the reaction be 80% complete ?
[Given : log 2 = \(0{\cdot}30\), log 3 = \(0{\cdot}48\), log 4 = \(0{\cdot}60\), log 5 = \(0{\cdot}69\)]
rows.solution:
FIRST PART — the rate constant. 25% complete means 75% of the reactant remains, so the ratio is \(100/75 = 4/3\):
\(k = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{40}\log\dfrac{4}{3}\)
\(= \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{40}(\log 4 - \log 3) = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{40}(0{\cdot}60 - 0{\cdot}48) = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303 \times 0{\cdot}12}{40}\)

\(k = 0{\cdot}0069\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

SECOND PART — time for 80% completion. Now 20% remains, so the ratio is \(100/20 = 5\):
\(t = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k}\log 5 = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303 \times 0{\cdot}69}{0{\cdot}0069}\)

\(t = 230{\cdot}3\ \mathrm{min}\)

Note what goes into the ratio: the fraction REMAINING, not the fraction reacted. Writing \(\log(100/25)\) for the first part is the commonest error here, and it would have given an answer nearly four times too large.

rows.stem:
(a) What type of nucleophilic substitution (\(\mathrm{S_N1}\) or \(\mathrm{S_N2}\)) occurs in the hydrolysis of 2-Bromobutane to form \((\pm)\)-Butan-2-ol ? Give reason.
(b) What happens when chlorobenzene and methyl chloride are treated with sodium metal in dry ether ?
rows.solution:
(a) The hydrolysis proceeds by \(\mathrm{S_N}1\).

The product is stated to be \((\pm)\)-butan-2-ol — a RACEMIC mixture, equal amounts of both enantiomers. That result is the signature of the unimolecular route.

In \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) the halide leaves first, giving a PLANAR carbocation. Being flat, it can be attacked by the nucleophile from EITHER FACE with equal ease, so the two enantiomers are formed in equal amounts and the product is optically inactive.

\(\mathrm{S_N}2\) would have given the opposite result. There the nucleophile attacks from the side directly opposite the leaving group, in one step, so the configuration is INVERTED and a single enantiomer results — not a racemate. Butan-2-yl bromide is secondary, which is exactly the class that can take either route depending on conditions; the stereochemistry reported is what identifies which one operated.

(b) TOLUENE is formed — the WURTZ-FITTIG reaction.

Sodium in dry ether couples an ARYL halide with an ALKYL halide, joining the two carbon skeletons directly:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5Cl} + \mathrm{CH_3Cl} + 2\mathrm{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CH_3} + 2\mathrm{NaCl}\)

Two side products accompany it, from the two halides coupling with themselves: diphenyl, by the Fittig reaction, and ethane, by the plain Wurtz reaction. All three appear in the flask, which is why the method is of limited preparative value.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the equations of the reactions involved in the following :
(i) Reimer-Tiemann reaction
(ii) Kolbe's reaction
(b) Name the reagent used in the bromination of phenol to form 2,4,6-Tribromophenol.
rows.solution:
(a)(i) REIMER-TIEMANN REACTION. Chloroform with aqueous alkali generates DICHLOROCARBENE, which attacks the phenoxide ion at its ORTHO position; acidification then frees the aldehyde:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H^+}]{1.\ \mathrm{CHCl_3} + \text{aq. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{o\text{-}HO{-}C_6H_4{-}CHO}\)
The product is salicylaldehyde. The alkali is needed twice over — to make the carbene and to convert phenol into the more strongly activated phenoxide ion.

(ii) KOLBE'S REACTION. Phenol is first converted to sodium phenoxide, which attacks CARBON DIOXIDE at its ortho position; acidification then frees the acid:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5O^-Na^+} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H^+}]{1.\ \mathrm{CO_2}} \mathrm{o\text{-}HO{-}C_6H_4{-}COOH}\)
The product is salicylic acid — the starting material for aspirin.

The two reactions are the same idea with different electrophiles: phenoxide is nucleophilic enough to attack even a feeble electrophile, and both attacks go ORTHO.

(b) The reagent is BROMINE WATER — bromine in aqueous solution.

Water is what makes all three positions substitute at once. It lets the phenol ionise to phenoxide, which is even more strongly activating than phenol itself, and no catalyst is needed. The white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol appears immediately.

Bromine in a NON-polar solvent such as carbon disulphide, at low temperature, stops after ONE substitution and gives a mixture of the ortho and para isomers — same reagent, different medium, different product.

rows.stem:
How will you bring about the following conversions ? (any three)
(a) Benzoic acid to Benzaldehyde
(b) Ethanal to Propanone
(c) Acetophenone to Benzoic acid
(d) Bromobenzene to 1-Phenylethanol
rows.solution:
(a) BENZOIC ACID TO BENZALDEHYDE, in two steps — the ROSENMUND route. The acid is first converted to its acyl chloride, which is then reduced under conditions mild enough to stop at the aldehyde:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{SOCl_2}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COCl} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{BaSO_4}]{\mathrm{H_2}/\mathrm{Pd}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}\)
The palladium is deliberately POISONED with barium sulphate; an unpoisoned catalyst would carry the reduction on to benzyl alcohol.

(b) ETHANAL TO PROPANONE, in two steps. Count the carbons: two in, three out, so a carbon must be ADDED — which a Grignard reagent does.
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H^+}/\mathrm{H_2O}]{1.\ \mathrm{CH_3MgBr}} \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{PCC}} \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\)
The Grignard turns the aldehyde into a SECONDARY alcohol, and oxidising a secondary alcohol gives a ketone.

(c) ACETOPHENONE TO BENZOIC ACID, by drastic oxidation. Alkaline permanganate cleaves the side chain right down to the carboxyl group, and acidification frees the acid:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KMnO_4}/\mathrm{KOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOK} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\)

(d) BROMOBENZENE TO 1-PHENYLETHANOL, in two steps. The halide is first converted to a Grignard reagent, which then adds to ethanal:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5Br} \xrightarrow[\text{dry ether}]{\mathrm{Mg}} \mathrm{C_6H_5MgBr} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H_3O^+}]{1.\ \mathrm{CH_3CHO}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CH(OH)CH_3}\)
An ALDEHYDE other than methanal gives a SECONDARY alcohol, which is what the target is.

rows.stem:
Give the structures of A, B and C in the following reactions :
(a) \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2Cl} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KCN}} \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{LiAlH_4}} \mathrm{B} \xrightarrow[0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}]{\mathrm{HNO_2}} \mathrm{C}\)
(b) Nitrobenzene \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Fe/HCl}} \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow[273\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{NaNO_2 + HCl}} \mathrm{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{C_6H_5OH}} \mathrm{C}\)
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — REQUIRED for sub-part (b) only - its starting material is printed as a DRAWN benzene ring carrying an \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) group, which is named 'Nitrobenzene' above rather than approximated. Sub-part (a) is printed entirely as a linear formula chain and is transcribed literally. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
(a) Potassium cyanide substitutes for the chloride, giving the NITRILE, and the carbon count rises from two to three:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CN}\), propanenitrile

Lithium aluminium hydride reduces a nitrile all the way to a PRIMARY AMINE, the carbon count unchanged:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2}\), propan-1-amine

Nitrous acid at \(0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) diazotises a primary ALIPHATIC amine, and the diazonium salt formed is unstable even at that temperature — it loses nitrogen at once and the cation picks up water:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH}\), propan-1-ol

(b) Iron with hydrochloric acid reduces the nitro group to an amino group:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\), aniline

Nitrous acid at 273 K diazotises it, and here the salt SURVIVES, because the ring delocalises the positive charge:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-}\), benzenediazonium chloride

Coupling that with phenol gives an AZO DYE, the diazonium ion attacking the phenol at its para position:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{C_6H_5{-}N{=}N{-}C_6H_4{-}OH}\), p-hydroxyazobenzene, an orange dye

The pair of sequences is a lesson in the difference between aliphatic and aromatic diazotisation: the same reagent destroys one substrate's diazonium salt and preserves the other's.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Why do transition metals and their compounds act as good catalysts ?
rows.context:
The involvement of \((n-1)d\) electrons in the behaviour of transition elements impart certain distinct characteristics to these elements. Thus, in addition to variable oxidation states, they exhibit paramagnetic behaviour, catalytic properties and tendency for the formation of coloured ions. The transition metals react with a number of non-metals like oxygen, nitrogen and halogens. \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) and \(\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}\) are common examples.
The two series of inner transition elements, lanthanoids and actinoids, constitute the f-block of the periodic table. In the lanthanoids, there is regular decrease in atomic size with increase in atomic number due to the imperfect shielding effect of 4f-orbital electrons which causes contraction.
rows.solution:
Because of their VARIABLE OXIDATION STATES and their ability to form COMPLEXES, together with the large SURFACE AREA that a finely divided metal provides.

A catalyst works by offering a lower-energy path, and a transition metal does that in two ways. Moving between oxidation states, it can accept electrons from one reactant and pass them to another, returning to its original state at the end — vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process works exactly this way, dropping to vanadium(IV) and being reoxidised by air.

The second route is ADSORPTION. Vacant d orbitals let the metal bind reactant molecules to its surface, holding them close together in the right orientation and weakening their bonds. Iron in the Haber process works this way, and it is used finely divided so that as much surface as possible is exposed.

rows.stem: What is the cause of contraction in the atomic size of lanthanoids ?
rows.context:
The involvement of \((n-1)d\) electrons in the behaviour of transition elements impart certain distinct characteristics to these elements. Thus, in addition to variable oxidation states, they exhibit paramagnetic behaviour, catalytic properties and tendency for the formation of coloured ions. The transition metals react with a number of non-metals like oxygen, nitrogen and halogens. \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) and \(\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}\) are common examples.
The two series of inner transition elements, lanthanoids and actinoids, constitute the f-block of the periodic table. In the lanthanoids, there is regular decrease in atomic size with increase in atomic number due to the imperfect shielding effect of 4f-orbital electrons which causes contraction.
rows.solution:
The cause is the POOR SHIELDING EFFECT OF THE \(4f\) ORBITALS.

Across the lanthanoid series each added electron goes into a \(4f\) orbital. Those orbitals are diffuse and irregularly shaped, so they screen the outer electrons from the nucleus badly — much less effectively than an \(s\) or \(p\) orbital would.

Each added proton therefore pulls the outer electrons in a little harder than the added electron pushes them out, and the net effect accumulates: the radius shrinks steadily from lanthanum to lutetium.

The same mechanism, with the even more diffuse \(5f\) orbitals, makes the actinoid contraction STEEPER still from one element to the next.

rows.stem: Define lanthanoid contraction. How does it affect the atomic radii of the third transition series and the second transition series ?
rows.context:
The involvement of \((n-1)d\) electrons in the behaviour of transition elements impart certain distinct characteristics to these elements. Thus, in addition to variable oxidation states, they exhibit paramagnetic behaviour, catalytic properties and tendency for the formation of coloured ions. The transition metals react with a number of non-metals like oxygen, nitrogen and halogens. \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) and \(\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}\) are common examples.
The two series of inner transition elements, lanthanoids and actinoids, constitute the f-block of the periodic table. In the lanthanoids, there is regular decrease in atomic size with increase in atomic number due to the imperfect shielding effect of 4f-orbital electrons which causes contraction.
rows.solution:
LANTHANOID CONTRACTION is the overall DECREASE in atomic and ionic radii across the lanthanoid series, from lanthanum to lutetium, as the atomic number increases. Its cause is the poor shielding of the nuclear charge by the \(4f\) electrons.

EFFECT ON THE TRANSITION SERIES. The fourteen lanthanoids lie between the second and third transition series in the periodic table, so the third series sits BEHIND all of that accumulated shrinkage.

The result is that the atomic radii of the SECOND and THIRD transition series are VERY NEARLY EQUAL — where one would have expected the third to be considerably larger, being a whole period below. The contraction almost exactly cancels that expected increase.

Zirconium and hafnium are the famous pair, at about 160 pm each; niobium and tantalum are another. Because chemical separation depends on differences in size, such pairs are notoriously difficult to separate.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: In aqueous media, which is a stronger reducing agent — \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) or \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) and why ?
rows.context:
The involvement of \((n-1)d\) electrons in the behaviour of transition elements impart certain distinct characteristics to these elements. Thus, in addition to variable oxidation states, they exhibit paramagnetic behaviour, catalytic properties and tendency for the formation of coloured ions. The transition metals react with a number of non-metals like oxygen, nitrogen and halogens. \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) and \(\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}\) are common examples.
The two series of inner transition elements, lanthanoids and actinoids, constitute the f-block of the periodic table. In the lanthanoids, there is regular decrease in atomic size with increase in atomic number due to the imperfect shielding effect of 4f-orbital electrons which causes contraction.
rows.solution:
\(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) is the stronger reducing agent.

A reducing agent gives electrons away, so the question is which ion loses an electron more readily — and that depends on what it BECOMES.

\(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) is \(3d^4\). Losing an electron gives \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\), which is \(3d^3\) — in an octahedral aqueous environment the stable half-filled \(t_{2g}^3\) arrangement, with one electron in each of the three lower orbitals. Chromium(II) therefore gives that electron up eagerly.

\(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is \(3d^6\). Losing an electron gives \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\), which is \(3d^5\) — also a stable half-filled arrangement, but of the whole d set rather than of the lower group. In aqueous solution, where the ligand field splits the orbitals, the \(t_{2g}^3\) configuration is the more favoured of the two.

The potentials bear it out: \(E^{\circ}\) for \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}/Cr^{2+}}\) is \(-0{\cdot}41\) V while that for \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}\) is \(+0{\cdot}77\) V — chromium(II) reduces even water, while iron(II) is stable in it.

rows.stem: What are essential amino acids ?
rows.context:
Proteins are the most abundant biomolecules of the living system. Proteins are the polymers of about twenty different \(\alpha\)-amino acids which are linked by peptide bonds. Ten amino acids are called essential amino acids. In zwitter ionic form, amino acids show amphoteric behaviour as they react both with acids and bases.
On the basis of their molecular shape, proteins are classified into two types : Fibrous and Globular proteins. Structure and shape of proteins can be studied at four different levels i.e., primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary, each level being more complex than the previous one. The secondary or tertiary structure of proteins get disturbed on change of pH or temperature and they are not able to perform their functions. This is called denaturation of proteins.
rows.solution:
ESSENTIAL AMINO ACIDS are those the body CANNOT synthesise for itself; they have to be supplied in the diet. Valine, leucine, isoleucine, lysine and phenylalanine are among them.

The contrast is with NON-ESSENTIAL amino acids, such as glycine and alanine, which the body can make from other materials.

Note that the name describes what the DIET must supply, not how important the acid is — both kinds are needed for protein synthesis, and a protein cannot be built if any one residue is missing. A protein food supplying all the essential acids in useful proportions is said to be of high biological value.

rows.stem: What is meant by zwitter ionic form of amino acids ?
rows.context:
Proteins are the most abundant biomolecules of the living system. Proteins are the polymers of about twenty different \(\alpha\)-amino acids which are linked by peptide bonds. Ten amino acids are called essential amino acids. In zwitter ionic form, amino acids show amphoteric behaviour as they react both with acids and bases.
On the basis of their molecular shape, proteins are classified into two types : Fibrous and Globular proteins. Structure and shape of proteins can be studied at four different levels i.e., primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary, each level being more complex than the previous one. The secondary or tertiary structure of proteins get disturbed on change of pH or temperature and they are not able to perform their functions. This is called denaturation of proteins.
rows.solution:
A ZWITTER ION is the form an amino acid takes in the solid state and in aqueous solution: a DIPOLAR ion carrying BOTH a positive and a negative centre, but NO net charge.

The carboxyl group of an amino acid is acidic enough to lose its proton and the amino group basic enough to take it, so the proton transfers WITHIN the molecule:
\(\mathrm{R{-}CH(NH_2){-}COOH} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{R{-}CH(\overset{+}{N}H_3){-}COO^-}\)

The carboxyl becomes \(-\mathrm{COO^-}\) and the amino becomes \(-\mathrm{\overset{+}{N}H_3}\).

Two consequences follow. The ion can react in EITHER direction — the carboxylate end accepting a proton from an acid, the ammonium end giving one up to a base — which is what amphoteric behaviour means. And amino acids behave like ionic solids: high melting points, and solubility in water rather than in organic solvents.

rows.stem:
(i) Give one example each for Fibrous protein and Globular protein.
(ii) What type of linkages hold monomers of proteins together ?
rows.context:
Proteins are the most abundant biomolecules of the living system. Proteins are the polymers of about twenty different \(\alpha\)-amino acids which are linked by peptide bonds. Ten amino acids are called essential amino acids. In zwitter ionic form, amino acids show amphoteric behaviour as they react both with acids and bases.
On the basis of their molecular shape, proteins are classified into two types : Fibrous and Globular proteins. Structure and shape of proteins can be studied at four different levels i.e., primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary, each level being more complex than the previous one. The secondary or tertiary structure of proteins get disturbed on change of pH or temperature and they are not able to perform their functions. This is called denaturation of proteins.
rows.solution:
(i) FIBROUS PROTEIN: KERATIN, found in hair, wool and nails. Myosin, in muscle, is another.
GLOBULAR PROTEIN: INSULIN, the hormone. Albumin, in egg white, is another.

The difference is in the shape of the chain. A fibrous protein has its chains running parallel to one another, held side by side, giving a thread-like structure that is insoluble in water; a globular protein has its chain coiled and folded into a roughly spherical shape and is soluble.

(ii) PEPTIDE LINKAGES hold the monomers together — the amide bond \(-\mathrm{CO-NH}-\) formed when the carboxyl group of one amino acid condenses with the amino group of the next, losing a molecule of water.

That linkage fixes the sequence of residues, which is the protein's PRIMARY structure. The higher levels of structure are held by weaker forces — hydrogen bonds, disulphide bridges and the like — which is why denaturation destroys them while leaving the primary structure intact.

rows.stem:
(i) What is the structural feature which characterises a reducing sugar ?
(ii) What is the structural difference between nucleoside and nucleotide ?
rows.context:
Proteins are the most abundant biomolecules of the living system. Proteins are the polymers of about twenty different \(\alpha\)-amino acids which are linked by peptide bonds. Ten amino acids are called essential amino acids. In zwitter ionic form, amino acids show amphoteric behaviour as they react both with acids and bases.
On the basis of their molecular shape, proteins are classified into two types : Fibrous and Globular proteins. Structure and shape of proteins can be studied at four different levels i.e., primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary, each level being more complex than the previous one. The secondary or tertiary structure of proteins get disturbed on change of pH or temperature and they are not able to perform their functions. This is called denaturation of proteins.
rows.solution:
(i) A reducing sugar has a FREE ALDEHYDIC OR KETONIC GROUP — equivalently, an ANOMERIC CARBON whose hydroxyl is not tied up in a glycosidic linkage.

Such a ring can open in solution to the straight-chain form and expose that carbonyl group, and it is the exposed group which reduces Tollens' reagent or Fehling's solution.

All monosaccharides qualify, and so do maltose and lactose, where one anomeric carbon is left free. SUCROSE does not: there the link runs between the anomeric carbons of BOTH units, neither ring can open, and no carbonyl group is ever exposed.

(ii) A NUCLEOSIDE has TWO components — a nitrogenous base joined to \(\mathrm{C_1}\) of a pentose sugar.

A NUCLEOTIDE has THREE — the same base and sugar, PLUS a phosphate group esterifying the hydroxyl at \(\mathrm{C_5}\) of the sugar.

The phosphate is the whole of the difference, and it is what makes the chain possible: it links the \(\mathrm{C_5}\) of one sugar to the \(\mathrm{C_3}\) of the next, building the backbone of a nucleic acid.

rows.stem:
(i) Calculate emf of the following cell at \(25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) :
\(\mathrm{Zn\,(s)}\,|\,\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\,(0{\cdot}001\mathrm{M})\,||\,\mathrm{Cd^{2+}}\,(0{\cdot}1\ \mathrm{M})\,|\,\mathrm{Cd\,(s)}\)
Given : \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} = -\,0{\cdot}76\) V, \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Cd^{2+}/Cd}} = -\,0{\cdot}40\) V   [log 10 = 1]
(ii) State Faraday's second law of electrolysis. How will the pH of aqueous NaCl solution be affected when it is electrolysed ?
rows.solution:
(i) Read the cell diagram: the ANODE is written on the left, so zinc is oxidised and cadmium deposited at the cathode.

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}} = (-0{\cdot}40) - (-0{\cdot}76) = 0{\cdot}36\ \mathrm{V}\)

The cell reaction is \(\mathrm{Zn} + \mathrm{Cd^{2+}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + \mathrm{Cd}\), so \(n = 2\) and the solids do not enter the quotient:
\(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{Cd^{2+}}]}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}36 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{0{\cdot}001}{0{\cdot}1} = 0{\cdot}36 - 0{\cdot}0295\log 10^{-2}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}36 - 0{\cdot}0295 \times (-2) = 0{\cdot}36 + 0{\cdot}059\)

\(E_{\text{cell}} = 0{\cdot}419\ \mathrm{V}\)

Note that the correction ADDS here, unlike most such problems. The product ion is at the LOWER concentration, which pushes the reaction forwards, so the logarithm is negative and the cell is slightly better than standard.

(ii) FARADAY'S SECOND LAW OF ELECTROLYSIS. When the same quantity of electricity is passed through different electrolytes connected in series, the amounts of the different substances liberated at the electrodes are proportional to their CHEMICAL EQUIVALENT WEIGHTS.

EFFECT ON pH: it RISES — the solution becomes alkaline.

At the cathode water is reduced in preference to the sodium ion, because its reduction potential is far less negative:
\(2\mathrm{H_2O} + 2e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{H_2} + 2\mathrm{OH^-}\)
Hydroxide ions accumulate, and with the sodium ions already present the product is sodium hydroxide. More hydroxide means a higher pH — which is why this electrolysis is the industrial source of caustic soda.

rows.stem:
(i) Calculate the \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}\mathrm{G^{o}}\) and \(\log \mathrm{K_c}\) for the following cell reaction :
\(\mathrm{Fe\,(s)} + \mathrm{Ag^{+}\,(aq)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Fe^{2+}(aq)} + \mathrm{Ag\,(s)}\)
Given : \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Fe^{2+}/Fe}} = -\,0{\cdot}44\) V, \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Ag^{+}/Ag}} = +\,0{\cdot}80\) V,
1 F = 96500 C \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)
(ii) Write any two advantages of the fuel cells over primary and secondary batteries ?
(iii) How many Faradays are required for the oxidation of 1 mole of \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) to \(\mathrm{O_2}\) ?
rows.solution:
(i) Silver has the more positive potential, so it is the cathode and iron the anode:
\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}} = 0{\cdot}80 - (-0{\cdot}44) = 1{\cdot}24\ \mathrm{V}\)

Iron goes from 0 to \(+2\), so TWO electrons are transferred and \(n = 2\). Note that the equation as printed needs balancing for that — two silver ions are reduced for each iron atom oxidised:
\(\mathrm{Fe(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Fe^{2+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{Ag(s)}\)

Free energy change:
\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = -2 \times 96500 \times 1{\cdot}24\)
\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -239320\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\), that is \(-239{\cdot}32\) kJ \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)

Equilibrium constant:
\(\log K_c = \dfrac{n\,E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}}}{0{\cdot}059} = \dfrac{2 \times 1{\cdot}24}{0{\cdot}059}\)
\(\log K_c = 42{\cdot}0\)

The sign is the check: a positive cell potential must give a negative free energy change and a very large equilibrium constant, and \(K_c \approx 10^{42}\) means the reaction goes essentially to completion.

(ii) TWO ADVANTAGES of fuel cells over primary and secondary batteries:

HIGH EFFICIENCY, around 70%, because the chemical energy is converted DIRECTLY into electrical energy instead of passing through heat, so the cell is not limited by the Carnot efficiency of a heat engine.

POLLUTION FREE — the hydrogen-oxygen cell produces only water, with no oxides of carbon, nitrogen or sulphur.

A third, if one is wanted: the cell does NOT RUN DOWN, because its reactants are supplied continuously from outside rather than stored within it, so it works as long as it is fed — unlike a primary battery, which is discarded, or a secondary one, which must be taken out of service to be recharged.

(iii) Write the half reaction and count electrons per molecule of water:
\(2\mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{O_2} + 4\mathrm{H^+} + 4e^-\)

Four electrons are released for every TWO molecules of water, so ONE mole of water requires 2 mol of electrons, and the charge is 2 FARADAY.

Reading four electrons straight off the equation and answering 4 F is the trap: that figure belongs to 2 mol of water, or equivalently to 1 mol of oxygen.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) Write the major product(s) in the following reactions :
(1) Ethylbenzene \(\xrightarrow[\mathrm{b)\ H^{+}}]{\mathrm{a)\ KMnO_4\,,\ KOH}}\) ?
(2) Benzaldehyde \(+\ \mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_3} \xrightarrow{\text{dil NaOH}}\) ?
(3) Benzoic acid \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2/FeBr_3}}\) ?
(ii) Give simple chemical tests to distinguish between the following pairs of compounds :
(1) Acetophenone and Propiophenone
(2) Pentanal and Pentan-3-one
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — REQUIRED - five of the compounds in this question are printed as DRAWN benzene-ring structures and are NAMED above rather than approximated: in (i)(1) a ring bearing \(\mathrm{CH_2CH_3}\) (ethylbenzene); in (i)(2) a ring bearing CHO (benzaldehyde), with its partner acetone printed out in full as \(\mathrm{CH_3-C(=O)-CH_3}\); in (i)(3) a ring bearing COOH (benzoic acid); and in (ii)(1) a ring bearing \(\mathrm{COCH_3}\) and a ring bearing \(\mathrm{COCH_2CH_3}\) (acetophenone and propiophenone). Pages idx 22 (stem through (i)(3)) and idx 24 ((ii)).
rows.solution:
(i)(1) Alkaline permanganate oxidises an alkyl side chain right down to the CARBOXYL group, whatever its length, provided the carbon attached to the ring carries at least one hydrogen. Acidification then frees the acid:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2CH_3} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H^+}]{1.\ \mathrm{KMnO_4},\ \mathrm{KOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\)
The product is BENZOIC ACID — the second carbon is lost entirely, which is what makes this a chain-shortening oxidation.

(2) Benzaldehyde has NO \(\alpha\)-hydrogen; propanone has six. So only the ketone can form the carbanion, and the CROSS ALDOL goes one way: the carbanion from propanone attacks the carbonyl of benzaldehyde. Dilute alkali WITHOUT heating stops at the addition product:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} + \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CH(OH)CH_2COCH_3}\)
The product is 4-hydroxy-4-phenylbutan-2-one. Heating would dehydrate it to the conjugated ketone.

(3) The carboxyl group is DEACTIVATING and META directing — it withdraws electron density from the ring, and most strongly from the ortho and para positions, which leaves the meta position relatively the richest:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2}/\mathrm{FeBr_3}} \mathrm{m\text{-}Br{-}C_6H_4{-}COOH}\)
The product is 3-bromobenzoic acid.

(ii)(1) Use the IODOFORM TEST. Warm each with sodium hydroxide and iodine: ACETOPHENONE has a \(\mathrm{CH_3CO}-\) group and gives a yellow precipitate of iodoform; PROPIOPHENONE has an ethyl group on its carbonyl instead, so it gives none.

The test detects a methyl group ON the carbonyl specifically, which is exactly what separates these two.

(2) Use TOLLENS' REAGENT. Warm each with ammoniacal silver nitrate: PENTANAL, being an aldehyde, is oxidised and deposits a silver mirror; PENTAN-3-ONE, being a ketone, does not react.

Fehling's solution serves equally well, giving a red precipitate with the aldehyde only. Note the iodoform test would be useless here — neither compound has a methyl group on its carbonyl.

rows.stem:
(i) Give reasons for the following :
(1) In semicarbazide, only one \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group is involved in the formation of semicarbazone.
(2) Acetaldehyde is more reactive than acetone towards addition of HCN.
(ii) (1) Arrange the following in decreasing order of their acidic strength :
\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\), \(\mathrm{O_2N-CH_2-COOH}\), \(\mathrm{HCOOH}\)
(2) Name the reagent in the following reaction :
\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH-CH_2-CN} \xrightarrow{?} \mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH-CH_2-CHO}\)
(iii) Write the reaction involved in Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction.
rows.solution:
(i)(1) Because one of the two amino groups is DEACTIVATED BY RESONANCE.

Semicarbazide is \(\mathrm{H_2N{-}NH{-}CO{-}NH_2}\), and one of its \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) groups is attached DIRECTLY to the carbonyl carbon. That nitrogen's lone pair is delocalised onto the carbonyl oxygen, so it is not available for attacking anything — it is an amide nitrogen, and amide nitrogens are poor nucleophiles.

The other \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\), the terminal one, is separated from the carbonyl by an intervening nitrogen and takes no part in that delocalisation. Its lone pair is free, so it is the one that attacks the aldehyde or ketone and forms the semicarbazone.

(2) Because the carbonyl carbon of acetaldehyde is MORE ELECTROPHILIC and LESS CROWDED.

Addition of hydrogen cyanide begins with the cyanide ion attacking that carbon, so the more positive and the more accessible it is, the faster the reaction. Acetone carries TWO methyl groups on its carbonyl carbon; acetaldehyde carries one methyl and one hydrogen.

Each methyl group RELEASES electron density by its inductive effect, reducing the positive charge on the carbon, and each one physically blocks the nucleophile's approach. Both effects run the same way, and acetone has twice as much of each.

(ii)(1) Decreasing acidic strength:
\(\mathrm{O_2N{-}CH_2{-}COOH} > \mathrm{HCOOH} > \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)

The nitro compound is by far the strongest: the nitro group is powerfully electron withdrawing, so it disperses the carboxylate's negative charge and stabilises the anion. Methanoic acid comes next — it carries only a HYDROGEN where the others have a carbon group, and hydrogen neither releases nor withdraws. Ethanoic acid is the weakest, its METHYL group releasing electron density and concentrating the charge.

(2) The reagent is DIBAL-H, diisobutylaluminium hydride, followed by hydrolysis.

DIBAL-H is a PARTIAL reducing agent: it takes a nitrile only as far as the imine, and hydrolysis of the imine gives the ALDEHYDE. A stronger reducing agent such as lithium aluminium hydride would carry the reduction on to the amine, and would also attack the carbon-carbon double bond that must survive here.

(iii) HELL-VOLHARD-ZELINSKY REACTION. A carboxylic acid carrying an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen is treated with chlorine or bromine in the presence of a small amount of RED PHOSPHORUS; hydrolysis then gives the \(\alpha\)-halo acid:
\(\mathrm{R{-}CH_2{-}COOH} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H_2O}]{1.\ \mathrm{X_2}/\text{red P}} \mathrm{R{-}CH(X){-}COOH}\) where \(\mathrm{X} = \mathrm{Cl}\) or \(\mathrm{Br}\)

The phosphorus is essential: it converts the acid into its acyl halide, which ENOLISES far more readily than the acid itself, and it is the enol that the halogen attacks. The \(\alpha\)-halo acid produced is a markedly stronger acid than the one it came from.

rows.stem:
Attempt any five of the following :
(a) Write the IUPAC name of the complex :
\([\mathrm{Co(H_2O)(CN)(en)_2}]^{2+}\)
(b) Why is geometrical isomerism not possible in tetrahedral complexes having two different types of unidentate ligands coordinated with the central metal ion ?
(c) Arrange the following complex ions in increasing order of their crystal field splitting energy \((\Delta_{\mathrm{o}})\) :
\([\mathrm{Co(NH_3)_6}]^{3+}\), \([\mathrm{CoF_6}]^{3-}\), \([\mathrm{Co(CN)_6}]^{3-}\)
(d) Write the hybridization and magnetic character of the complex \([\mathrm{Ni(CO)_4}]\) on the basis of valence bond theory.
[Atomic No. : Ni = 28]
(e) Out of \([\mathrm{CoF_6}]^{3-}\) and \([\mathrm{Co(C_2O_4)_3}]^{3-}\), which one complex is :
(i) more stable ?
(ii) the high spin complex ?
(f) What is the difference between an ambidentate ligand and bidentate ligand ?
(g) Write the electronic configuration of \(\mathrm{d^5}\) in terms of \(\mathrm{t_{2g}}\) and \(\mathrm{e_g}\) in an octahedral field when :
(i) \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}} > \mathrm{P}\),   and   (ii) \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}} < \mathrm{P}\)
rows.solution:
(a) The cyanido ligand gives \(-1\), water and the two diamines are neutral, and the ion carries \(+2\), so cobalt is \(+3\). Ligands are named alphabetically — aqua, then cyanido, then the diamine, which takes bis- because its own name already contains a numerical prefix:
AQUACYANIDOBIS(ETHANE-1,2-DIAMINE)COBALT(III) ION

(b) Because in a TETRAHEDRAL complex every position is ADJACENT to every other.

Geometrical isomerism requires two ligands to be distinguishable as "next to" or "opposite" one another. In an octahedron each position has four neighbours and one opposite, so cis and trans are genuinely different. In a tetrahedron all four corners are equidistant from one another — there is no "opposite" position at all — so any two unidentate ligands are in the same relative arrangement however they are placed.

(c) Increasing crystal field splitting energy:
\([\mathrm{CoF_6}]^{3-} < [\mathrm{Co(NH_3)_6}]^{3+} < [\mathrm{Co(CN)_6}]^{3-}\)

The metal and its oxidation state are the same throughout, so the LIGAND alone decides. The spectrochemical series orders ligands by the splitting they produce, and in it fluoride is a weak field ligand, ammonia intermediate, and cyanide one of the strongest known.

(d) In \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) nickel is in the ZERO oxidation state, \(3d^8 4s^2\). Carbon monoxide drives the two \(4s\) electrons into the \(3d\) set, giving \(3d^{10}\) with every electron paired and no inner orbital free; bonding must then use the \(4s\) and all three \(4p\).

Hybridisation \(sp^3\), so the geometry is tetrahedral; with no unpaired electron the complex is DIAMAGNETIC.

(e)(i) MORE STABLE: \([\mathrm{Co(C_2O_4)_3}]^{3-}\).
The oxalate ion is BIDENTATE, so each ligand closes a five-membered CHELATE RING around the metal. A chelating ligand binds far more firmly than the same number of separate donors would — the chelate effect — so this complex is much the more stable of the two.

(ii) HIGH SPIN: \([\mathrm{CoF_6}]^{3-}\).
Fluoride is a WEAK field ligand: the splitting it produces is smaller than the pairing energy, so the six d electrons of \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) spread out as \(t_{2g}^4\,e_g^2\) with four unpaired. Oxalate lies higher in the spectrochemical series and gives the low spin arrangement.

(f) An AMBIDENTATE ligand has TWO DIFFERENT donor atoms but binds through only ONE of them at a time — the nitrite ion through nitrogen or through oxygen, the thiocyanate ion through sulphur or through nitrogen. The choice gives rise to LINKAGE isomerism.

A BIDENTATE ligand binds the metal through TWO donor atoms AT THE SAME TIME, closing a chelate ring — ethane-1,2-diamine through both its nitrogens, the oxalate ion through two of its oxygens.

The distinction is between having a CHOICE of two atoms and USING two atoms at once.

(g)(i) \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}} > \mathrm{P}\) means the splitting costs MORE than pairing, so electrons fill the lower set completely before any goes up:
\(t_{2g}^5\,e_g^0\) — one unpaired electron, a LOW SPIN complex.

(ii) \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}} < \mathrm{P}\) means pairing is the dearer of the two, so electrons spread out singly over all five orbitals:
\(t_{2g}^3\,e_g^2\) — five unpaired electrons, a HIGH SPIN complex.
